slides: Open by naming the theorem's bridge: integration turns calculus objects into topology functionals. Chapter 17 made de Rham cohomology look topological; this chapter identifies it with real singular cohomology by integrating smooth forms over smooth singular chains.

Start at chain level because the proof rests on signs. A singular chain is a formal sum of simplex maps, and the alternating boundary signs are what make boundary squared equal zero. The check multiplies the boundary matrices and gets the zero column.

The integration pairing needs smooth simplices, so the chapter explains why smooth singular homology is enough. The smoothing picture keeps endpoints and faces fixed while replacing a kinked simplex by a smooth one. The second-difference spike drops from about 0.00200 to about 0.000208.

This is the local compatibility engine. On the standard triangle, the form x dy has exterior derivative dx wedge dy. The area integral is one half, and only the slanted edge contributes one half to the boundary integral, so Stokes holds at the chain level.

The de Rham homomorphism sends a closed form class to the functional that integrates it over smooth cycles. On the circle, the normalized angular form pairs with cycles exactly by winding number: positive generator one, reversed generator minus one, constant cycle zero, twice around two.

The proof needs the integration map to commute with more than individual cycles. The compatibility graph shows the wiring: smooth forms and smooth chains feed integration, Stokes makes it descend to cohomology, naturality and Mayer-Vietoris squares commute, and those squares feed the five lemma.

Use this slide to make the five-lemma step tangible. If two exact rows are connected by vertical maps and the surrounding four vertical maps are isomorphisms, the middle map is forced to be an isomorphism. The check records exact rows, left and right pairs of isomorphisms, and the middle forced isomorphism.

The proof is local-to-global. Convex open sets are handled by the Poincare lemma and point homology; two-set covers are handled by Mayer-Vietoris and the five lemma; finite covers repeat the two-set step; arbitrary manifolds come from locally finite countable constructions.

The applied lab is a sanity test for the theorem's dependencies. If boundary signs are changed, boundary squared will fail; if a nonsmooth simplex is used without smoothing, pulling back forms is not justified; if Stokes compatibility is dropped, exact forms no longer automatically define zero singular cochains.

Close by summarizing the theorem without losing the mechanics. Singular homology supplies cycles, singular cohomology supplies functionals, smooth chains allow integration, Stokes makes integration a cochain map, and Mayer-Vietoris plus the five lemma prove the integration map is an isomorphism.
